citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
A VMO observed following animals in need of veterinary care:
** One elderly pig housed indoors was observed with very little hair. Her skin was rough, red, and thickened, with several
dark red areas on her side. She appeared underweight, with some hip bones and spine visible. Previously, she was being
fed a specialized diet for senior pigs. However representatives stated she was no longer receiving any special diet, but
they were applying coconut oil onto the skin regularly. The attending veterinarian stated that she was aware the facility
owned an elderly pig, but does not recall performing an exam on the animal and is not aware of her health status.
** One adult black sheep and one adult brown and white goat housed in an indoor enclosure appeared underweight. Ribs,
hip bones, and spine were easily visible with minimal fat around the belly and sides. Neither facility representatives nor
the attending veterinarian could recall information about their health status, and they had not received diagnostics or
treatments.
** One adult African pygmy goat had abnormal hooves, especially front right hoof which was curving upwards. This could
lead to hoof pain or abnormal walking.
Failing to diagnose, control, and treat disease or injury places animals at risk for pain, discomfort, and worsening physical
conditions.
The facility took measures to correct this at the time of inspection (purchased senior pig feed and trimmed hooves). The
animals in need of veterinary care must be evaluated by a veterinarian for treatment. The facility must use appropriate
methods to prevent, control, diagnose, and treat diseases and injuries, and ensure the availability of emergency,
weekend, and holiday care. Correction date: 8/31/2026.

The facility’s record of dispositions was incomplete.
The facility was missing disposition records for six adult goats and birth records of five 2-3 week old baby goats. When
asked about the six goat dispositions, representatives and recalled that in the past few months, two employees purchased
one goat each and 2-3 months ago, one goat had died. There were no disposition records for those goats.
Representatives could not recall disposition information regarding the three remaining goats.
Incomplete disposition records prevent tracing of animal gains and losses.
The facility created the disposition records after the inspection. Continue to correct by ensuring that records are created
and maintained which fully and correctly disclose information concerning animals in his or her possession or under his or
her control, or which is transported, sold, euthanized, or otherwise disposed of by that exhibitor. The records shall include
the date and number of offspring born while in possession, and date of disposal of the animals.
Correction date: 8/31/2026.

Several goats housed in an indoor enclosure were not handled as expeditiously or carefully as possible.
During the inspection, an inspector observed an adult goat that had escaped from its primary enclosure after a youth
summer camp attendee incompletely closed the gate. The goat had walked down the hallway and was attempting to eat
the horse's food. Facility representatives stated that goats occasionally escape their primary enclosure due to incomplete
gate closure.
Handling animals in a manner that leads to escape places animals at risk of injury and provides them access to items that
could be harmful to their health.
The goat was returned to the enclosure at the time of inspection. Ensure all animals are handled expeditiously and
carefully in a manner that does not cause trauma, behavioral stress, physical harm, or unnecessary discomfort.
Correction date: 8/31/2026.

The facility is not storing food and bedding supplies in a manner that adequately protects them from deterioration,
molding, or contamination by vermin. The findings are as follows:
** The loft which stores food and bedding contained numerous dusty items near the hay and had and numerous cobwebs
on several bales of hay. A representative stated the hay affected by the cobwebs would not be fed to the animals and
would be removed. However, this loft has no light source. The loft is so dark that the inspector was unable to visualize the
hay closely enough to assess its quality and check for vermin, pests, or insects. In order to see, a large door must be
opened to allow sunlight in. This door exposes the hay to rain and other elements.
** While assessing the grain fed to all animals (pigs, goats, sheep, zebu), a representative turned the wheel on the large
grain storage bin, which dispensed a handful of grain into the inspector’s hand. The dispensed grain contained a live
maggot. A representative stated that there is usually plywood over the top of the large grain bin to protect it, but the
plywood had been moved and had not been replaced.
Inadequate storage of food and bedding can expose animals to contaminants or vermin, or reduce feed quality.
Measures were taken to correct this at the time of inspection. Supplies of food and bedding shall be stored in facilities
which adequately protect such supplies against deterioration, molding, or contamination by vermin.
Correction date: 9/15/2026.

The indoor enclosure housing 16 goats, 22 sheep, 1 zebu, and several other non-USDA regulated animals (ponies,
donkeys) is not cleaned as often as necessary.
The facility uses pine shavings and straw as bedding. During the inspection, the bedding was a dark brown soft, spongy,
uneven, and damp mixture of excreta and bedding. Dried brown material was visible on the feet and fur/wool of a few
animals. The front of the enclosure near the water bowls was the most damp while some less congested areas near the
back were dry and spongy.
Representatives stated that the stalls are cleaned and mucked out twice weekly, but excessive rain drained into the
enclosure and accumulated moisture in the front. Employees began mucking the enclosure during the inspection and
revealed layers of dark brown material about 1 foot in depth.
Excessive accumulations of soiled bedding is a hazard for spreading contagious parasitic or bacterial diseases, and non-
contagious diseases such as foot and hoof conditions. The uneven flooring is a trip hazard for the animals.
Excreta shall be removed from primary enclosures as often as necessary to prevent contamination of the animals
contained therein, and to minimize disease hazards, and to reduce odors. Correction date: 8/31/2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with facility representatives.
